explanations.answer: To serve him under a treaty
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The men of Jabesh say, “Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.” They're surrounded, so they come with an offer to serve. Nobody in that town is asking for a fight.

No champion steps forward anywhere in this passage. What the men of Jabesh actually say is, “Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.” That's an offer to serve, not to duel. Surrounded and trying to talk it out, that's a tough spot to be in.

explanations.answer: To give him the town and leave
explanations.explanation: Nobody offers to pack up and walk away. The men of Jabesh say, “Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.” They plan to stay and serve under a treaty. I'd have loved a simple ending too, but that's not what the text gives.
Yes. Nahash the Ammonite says he'll do it “and bring reproach upon all Israel.” So it's bigger than one town under siege. This part is heavy, and I think the elders felt the weight of it.

The Philistines don't come up in these words from Nahash the Ammonite. He says his condition is meant to “bring reproach upon all Israel.” That's Israel as a whole, not one outside enemy. It's a heavy thing to say, so let's take it seriously.

Gibeah is where the messengers go later, but Nahash the Ammonite doesn't name it here. He says he wants to “bring reproach upon all Israel.” His words reach past Jabesh to the whole nation. That's a heavy line, friend.

I get why you'd think so, since the offer on the table is terrible. But the elders don't accept it. They answer, “Hold off for seven days…” and ask to send messengers throughout Israel. They're buying time to find someone who can save them.

Right, they don't take it. The elders of Jabesh say, “Hold off for seven days,” and ask to send messengers throughout Israel. They aren't ready to say yes yet. I'd want a few days to look for help too.

Yes, and they say it plainly: “If there is no one to save us, we will surrender to you.” The seven days are a window. They're looking for a rescuer, and the surrender is what happens if none shows up.

The elders do tell him that. After asking for seven days, they say, “If there is no one to save us, we will surrender to you.” So there's a deadline attached. Either someone comes to save them or they give in.
That's right, they “wept aloud.” The messengers relay the words from Jabesh in the hearing of the people, and the whole crowd breaks down. It was the kind of news that stops a town in its tracks.
Nobody's cheering in Gibeah. The messengers relay the words from Jabesh, and the people all weep aloud. The news was heavy, and the crowd responds to it that way.
The text doesn't say they prayed here. What it says is that they all wept aloud. Prayer may be a good guess for a worried town, but I'll only tell you what the verse gives.
Yes, “the Spirit of God rushed upon him.” Saul, Israel's new king, has just come in from the field and hears the news from Jabesh. The Spirit arrives and everything changes for him in that moment.

Fear isn't what rushes upon Saul. The text says “the Spirit of God rushed upon him.” This is Saul, Israel's new king, hearing the news from Jabesh for the first time. Something much bigger than a shiver comes over him.
No napping happens here. Saul has just come in from the field, and when he hears the words from Jabesh, the Spirit of God rushes upon him. He's wide awake after that, friend.
That's the word. Saul “burned with great anger.” The people around him are weeping, and Saul is burning. The text doesn't tell us more than that about what's going on inside him.
Sorrow fits the crowd, because they were weeping. But the text says of Saul that “he burned with great anger.” It's a different reaction from the people around him.
The text doesn't say Saul feels shame. It says that when the Spirit of God rushed upon him, “he burned with great anger.” Burning is a strong word, and the verse uses it for him.

explanations.answer: March behind Saul and Samuel or else
explanations.explanation: Yes, and the words are strong. Saul sends them out saying, “This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not march behind Saul and Samuel.” Samuel is Israel's prophet, and Saul puts his name right next to his own. Pieces of oxen are hard to ignore, friend.

explanations.answer: Pay the new king's tax or else
explanations.explanation: No taxes in this message. Saul sends the pieces with the words, “This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not march behind Saul and Samuel.” The call is to march. It has nothing to do with money, thank goodness.

explanations.answer: Send your oxen to Gibeah or else
explanations.explanation: Saul isn't collecting oxen. He's the one who cuts a pair of them into pieces and sends them out. The message says, “This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not march behind Saul and Samuel.” Marching is what he asks for.
I see the guess, but the count is huge. Saul numbers them at Bezek and finds 300,000 Israelites and 30,000 men of Judah. That is a LOT of people showing up.
Right, it's no small crowd. At Bezek, Saul numbers 300,000 Israelites and 30,000 men of Judah. I'd have needed a bigger counting table, friend.

explanations.answer: Tomorrow by the time the sun is hot
explanations.explanation: That's the promise. The messengers carry it home: “Deliverance will be yours tomorrow by the time the sun is hot.” That's a short wait after days of worrying. And the men of Jabesh rejoice when they hear it.

Seven days was what the elders asked Nahash for, back at the start. The promise sent home is much sooner: “Deliverance will be yours tomorrow by the time the sun is hot.” Sooner than anyone in Jabesh had counted on.
No moon is mentioned here. The promise is, “Deliverance will be yours tomorrow by the time the sun is hot.” That's tomorrow, and it's tied to the heat of the day.

explanations.answer: Tomorrow we'll come out to you
explanations.explanation: Yes. The men of Jabesh tell Nahash, “Tomorrow we will come out…” and add that he can do with them whatever seems good to him. Their words to him are about coming out. They say nothing yet about help on the way.

explanations.answer: Give us seven more days to decide
explanations.explanation: They don't ask for more time here. The seven days were the first request, back when they asked Nahash to hold off. This time the men of Jabesh say, “Tomorrow we will come out…” and name a day.

explanations.answer: Our king is marching here to fight
explanations.explanation: The men of Jabesh don't say that to Nahash. Their words are, “Tomorrow we will come out, and you can do with us whatever seems good to you.” Nothing about a king or an army comes up in what they say to him.
That's right. The survivors were “so scattered that no two of them were left together.” This is a heavy part of the story, and the text tells it plainly. The Ammonite camp is completely broken up.
The text says the opposite. The survivors were “so scattered that no two of them were left together.” That's a heavy part of the story, and it ends with the camp totally scattered.

Yes, and they say it outright: “Bring those men here so we can kill them!” The people are talking about the ones who asked, “Who said that Saul should not reign over us?” They've just seen a big win, and tempers are high.

They don't talk about sending anyone away. The people say, “Bring those men here so we can kill them!” That's a far heavier thing than being driven out. It's the people's words, and Saul has a response coming.
Bowing isn't what the people want. They say, “Bring those men here so we can kill them!” Those are strong words, and they set up what Saul says next.

It would be easy to guess he'd go along, since the people are fired up. But Saul says the opposite: “No one shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.” He doesn't order anyone brought out.

Right, he does not. Saul orders, “No one shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.” The crowd wants one thing and Saul says another. I'd have bet on the crowd, friend.
That's it. Saul says, “…for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.” Saul had just led the army, and he points to the LORD for the salvation. That's what he says in front of everybody.
Samuel, Israel's prophet, is part of this story, but Saul doesn't name him here. He says, “…for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.” The salvation is credited to the LORD.
Saul's army did just march, and no one's taking that from them. But Saul's words are, “…for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.” He gives the credit to the LORD, not to the troops.
Yes, Gilgal. Samuel says, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there.” Samuel is Israel's prophet, and he's the one leading the way. The people follow him there in verse 15.
Mizpah isn't the place named here. Samuel says, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there.” The text gives Gilgal as the destination.
Bethel doesn't come up in this passage. Samuel tells the people, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there.” Gilgal is the answer the verse gives.

That's the word. The text says that after the peace offerings before the LORD, “Saul and all the Israelites rejoiced greatly.” It's a big celebration after a long, tense stretch. Rejoicing greatly is exactly how this passage ends.

Mourning isn't how this passage ends. At Gilgal, they confirm Saul as king and offer peace offerings before the LORD. Then “Saul and all the Israelites rejoiced greatly.” The weeping from earlier in the passage is over by now.

No worrying at Gilgal. The people confirm Saul as king in the presence of the LORD and offer peace offerings. Then “Saul and all the Israelites rejoiced greatly.” For once, the whole crowd gets to breathe.
